name: Swansea
title: Swansea Thickness Measurement | UTM in the Docks and Drydocks
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Swansea for short-sea bulk carriers, cargo ships, tugs and dredgers: drydock renewal surveys, holds, tanks and piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging at Swansea Docks and Swansea Dry Docks
intro: Swansea's enclosed docks sit behind a lock on Swansea Bay, sheltered from one of the largest tidal ranges in the world, and handle bulk and general cargo for South Wales. The port is also home to Swansea Dry Docks, a ship-repair yard with two graving docks used by short-sea bulk carriers, harbour tugs and dredgers. Ships in dock for repair and ships alongside for cargo both give time for gauging. Technicians are sent from India for each job, to the dock floor or the cargo berth.

highlights.p: Swansea Dry Docks takes short-sea bulk carriers, tugs and dredgers into its two graving docks. With the hull dry, the team gauges shell, bottom and sea chests to the agreed plan while the class surveyor and the yard decide on renewals.

highlights.h: A lock that steadies the work
highlights.p: Inside the lock, ships lie in impounded water at a steady level, unaffected by the bay's large tidal range. Gangways stay put, staging stays level, and a cargo ship alongside can be gauged without stopping for the tide.

Tugs and aggregate dredgers wear in ways cargo ships do not: fendering and towing points on tugs, hoppers, suction pipes and pump casings on dredgers. UT and magnetic particle testing find the wastage and cracking before the next season's work.

port.h: Swansea: an enclosed dock system on a big-tide bay
p: Swansea lies at the mouth of the River Tawe on the north shore of Swansea Bay, where the Bristol Channel opens towards the Celtic Sea. The bay's tides are among the largest anywhere, so the commercial port, owned and run by Associated British Ports, is an enclosed system entered through a lock. Inside, the King's Dock and the Prince of Wales Dock hold the cargo berths and the drydocks, while the old South Dock nearer the city centre is now a marina. Ships approach across the bay and anchor off when they arrive early or must wait for the tide to work the lock, and pilots board in the approaches for the passage in.

The cargo is short-sea: dry bulks, steel, aggregates and other materials for the industries of South Wales, carried by coasters and small bulk carriers sized for the lock, together with project and general cargo. The drydocks bring a separate stream of ships that come to Swansea purely for repair: short-sea bulk carriers from Irish and other European owners, harbour tugs and dredgers, docked for routine maintenance and survey work, and, the yard says, for recycling as well. That mix of cargo calls and repair stays gives Swansea more gauging work than its size suggests, and the same ship may be seen here twice, once alongside with cargo and again on the blocks.

Seasons matter less here than tides and weather. Winter gales from the south-west roll up the Bristol Channel and can make the bay anchorage uncomfortable and delay arrivals at the lock, but once a ship is inside it lies in calm water. The Bristol Channel also carries a heavy load of silt, which settles in sea chests and strainers and wears sea-water pipework from the inside, so piping and sea chests deserve a place in most scopes here. For inspection planning, the questions are when the ship will lock in, how long the cargo or repair stay will last, and what the superintendent needs measured before it locks out again.

facilities.h: Drydocks, cargo berths and the bay anchorage at Swansea
p: Swansea Dry Docks has two graving docks, the larger known as Prince of Wales Dry Dock 1, and during 2025 it docked Irish-flagged short-sea bulk carriers back to back, a harbour tug and an aggregate suction dredger. A ship in dock here is the best opportunity for a complete scope: bottom and side shell, sea chests, rudder and stern frame, double bottom and the full tank and hold programme, with the yard providing staging and services. The team works for the owner or manager alongside the yard's schedule and the class surveyor's inspection, and marks substantial corrosion on the steel as it is found.

At the cargo berths in the King's Dock and the Prince of Wales Dock, ships alongside for loading or discharge are gauged around the stevedores: holds as they empty, hatch covers when open, ballast tanks once the crew can release them. A ship that has finished cargo and is waiting for orders or a lock window can stay longer at a lay-by berth, which suits a fuller survey scope. At anchor in Swansea Bay, launch boarding is possible in quiet weather, but the bay is open to the south-west and most owners prefer to wait until the ship is inside the lock.
list: Prince of Wales Dry Dock 1 — full renewal-survey and docking-survey gauging on short-sea bulk carriers and other ships in dock.
Second graving dock — shell, sea chest and tank gauging on tugs, dredgers and smaller ships under repair.
King's Dock and Prince of Wales Dock cargo berths — hold, hatch-cover and ballast tank readings during cargo work.
Lay-by berths inside the lock — longer scopes on ships waiting for orders, cargo or a repair slot.
Swansea Bay anchorage — deck and air-pipe readings by launch in settled weather only.

context.h: Port state control, recycling rules and repair work at Swansea
p: The Maritime and Coastguard Agency inspects foreign-flagged ships at Swansea within the Paris MoU, and short-sea bulk carriers and general cargo ships, often older and lightly crewed, draw close attention for hold, hatch and ballast tank condition. A ship arriving with known corrosion and a renewal plan is in a much stronger position than one where an inspector finds thin plating first. Many of the ships calling at Swansea are also on the way to or from the drydocks, and a short in-service gauging visit before docking can fix the steel list in time for the yard to order plate.

Swansea Dry Docks describes its business as repair, maintenance and recycling. Ship recycling in the UK is governed by the UK's own version of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, kept on the statute book after Brexit, which also expects foreign-flagged ships calling at UK ports to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials. For owners weighing a further round of repairs against recycling, thickness gauging gives the deciding figures: how much steel would have to be renewed to keep the ship in class, set against the trading life she still has in front of her.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Swansea
jobs.p: Work in Swansea divides between the drydocks and the cargo berths. In dock, scopes are large and tied to a survey and a yard programme; alongside, they are smaller and tied to cargo work or a wait for orders. In both cases we agree the plan with the superintendent first, and in dock with the yard and the class surveyor as well, so the readings arrive while decisions about steel are being made rather than afterwards. Tugs and dredgers come with scopes of their own, built around the wear their work causes. These are the jobs we see most often here.
list: Renewal-survey gauging on a short-sea bulk carrier in Swansea Dry Docks: shell, double bottom, holds and ballast tanks, worked with the yard and class.
Docking gauging on a harbour tug: shell plating at the fendering, sea chests, and MPI on towing hook and bollard foundations.
Aggregate dredger in dock: UT of hopper plating, suction pipe and pump casing wall thickness, where abrasion removes steel fastest.
Hold and hatch-cover gauging on a coaster during discharge in the King's Dock.
Condition gauging to inform a repair-or-recycle decision on an older ship already in the docks.

logistics: Cardiff Airport and Bristol Airport are the nearest international airports, and many teams arrive at Heathrow and take the train from London Paddington to Swansea. The docks are an ISPS-controlled port with gated access, so the ship's agent arranges passes, while the drydock issues its own site passes and induction for work in the dock. The team travels from India on UK visas, and drydock dates are usually fixed weeks ahead, which leaves time to secure visas before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a ship in Swansea Dry Docks for its owner?
faqs.a: Yes, as the owner's or manager's contractor. The superintendent arranges our place in the yard programme, and the yard provides staging, lighting and the gas-free certificates for tanks. We gauge to a measurement plan agreed beforehand with the class surveyor, report thin areas to the surveyor and superintendent as they are found, and paint locations needing renewal so the yard's steel gang can start without waiting for the report.

faqs.q: Does the lock or the tide limit when a ship can be gauged?
faqs.a: Only at the start and end of the stay. Ships lock in and out around the tide, so arrival and departure times move with it, but inside the lock the water level is steady and work alongside goes on regardless of the bay's tide. We plan the mobilisation around the expected lock-in time and keep in touch with the agent in case it moves.

faqs.q: Do you gauge tugs and dredgers as well as cargo ships?
faqs.a: Yes. On tugs we gauge shell plating, especially around the fendering and at the waterline, sea chests and deck structure, and use magnetic particle testing on towing hook and winch foundations. On dredgers the focus is abrasion: hopper plating, suction and discharge pipes and pump casings, where sand and gravel wear steel away much faster than corrosion does.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while cargo is worked in Swansea docks?
faqs.a: Hold by hold. Once a hold is empty and safe to enter, the team gauges side shell, frames, hopper and tank top plating while discharge carries on elsewhere. Hatch covers and coamings are read when they are open. Ballast tanks follow when the crew have ventilated them and issued an entry permit, which often fits after cargo completes and before the ship locks out.
